reading.body:
CyrusOne's Sterling, Virginia campus publishes 38 MW of IT capacity across 700,000 square feet, ranking 13th among the 25 Virginia facilities that disclose a capacity figure.

The disclosure itself is the pattern. Virginia has 330 mapped data center facilities, and only 25 publish a capacity number, so the 1,603 MW state total and Sterling's 2.4 percent share describe a small visible subset rather than the state's actual load. For AI, published IT capacity is the main public proxy for how much compute a building can host, which means the 305 facilities without a figure are unmeasured rather than small.

Sterling's 38 MW converts to roughly 950 racks only under an assumed 40 kW per rack, which is a modeling assumption, not a specification. The facility publishes no certifications, so nothing in the data states what workload classes it is qualified to host. Its suitability score of 69 is built from published IT capacity and operator type, and the one input flagged as missing is announced expansion.

What the data does not cover is the constraint that matters most. There is no grid figure, no interconnection status, no power purchase arrangement, and no expansion pipeline for Sterling or its region. The coordinates are unset, so the record does not even fix the site geographically. On this evidence, Sterling can be placed in Virginia's disclosed capacity ranking, but nothing here establishes whether its local grid can absorb more load.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
